title: Haverstraw Bay

{{short description|Widest portion of the Hudson River}}
{{Use American English|date=July 2025}}
[[Image:Haverstraw Bay.jpg|250px|thumb|right|Haverstraw Bay as seen from Haverstraw]]
'''Haverstraw Bay''', located in [[New York (state)|New York]], is the widest portion of the [[Hudson River]]. The width of Haverstraw Bay is approximately {{convert|3.4|miles}}, the length approximately {{convert|5|miles}} from river kilometer 58 (river mile 36) at Croton Point to river kilometer 66 (river mile 41) at Stony Point. The bay is bordered by the [[village]] of [[Haverstraw (village), New York|Haverstraw]], in [[Rockland County, New York|Rockland County]], to the west and the village of [[Croton-on-Hudson, New York|Croton-on-Hudson]], in [[Westchester County, New York|Westchester County]], to the east.{{Citation needed|date=December 2020}}

== Geography ==
{{maplink|frame-width=250|type=point|zoom=11|text=Location of bay in the Hudson River|frame=yes}}
Haverstraw Bay is bordered to the west by the [[town]] and village of [[Haverstraw]] and to the east by the northern portion of the town of [[Ossining (town), New York|Ossining]], village of [[Croton-on-Hudson]] and the southern portion of the town of [[Cortlandt, New York|Cortlandt]]. Haverstraw Bay is approximately 35 miles (56 kilometers) to the north of [[New York City]]. A major feature of the bay is the large [[peninsula]] that forms its southern downstream border, [[Croton Point]], which juts almost halfway across the Hudson from the eastern shore. Croton Point Park is a popular birding location, including  frequent sightings of the [[bald eagle]]. The moderately saline bay is the northern, upstream boundary of the lower Hudson River estuary.<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://training.fws.gov/library/pubs5/web_link/text/low_hud.htm |title=lower hudson estuary<!-- Bot generated title --> |access-date=2008-05-25 |archive-date=2008-09-05 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080905143200/http://training.fws.gov/library/pubs5/web_link/text/low_hud.htm |url-status=dead }}</ref>

== Ecology ==
The bay's physical and biological characteristics make it one of the most significant [[estuarine]] areas in the [[Hudson River]].  The bay is deeper on its western side with a shipping channel of minimum 32 feet in depth and 300 feet in width. The bay's eastern side is shallower with most of that section of bay not more than 10 feet deep.<ref>MapTech Hudson River, Chart 4, Edition 5, 2003.</ref> Shallow depths with ample sunlight lead to robust aquatic vegetation. Inflows of brackish Atlantic Ocean water overlaid with fresh stream water promote a nutrient rich environment for myriad invertebrate, fish, and bird species. The bay's ecology plays a central role in the health of fish populations in the Hudson River, including the endangered [[shortnose sturgeon]] and the larger, more abundant [[atlantic sturgeon]]. New York State has designated Haverstraw Bay a "Significant Coastal Fish and Wildlife Habitat".<ref name="nyswaterfronts">{{cite web|url=http://www.nyswaterfronts.com/waterfront_natural_narratives.asp|title=Natural Waterfront - Natural Resources|accessdate=2010-11-07|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20100926161825/http://nyswaterfronts.com/waterfront_natural_narratives.asp|archivedate=2010-09-26}}</ref><ref name="rating">{{cite web|format=pdf|url=http://www.nyswaterfronts.com/downloads/pdfs/sig_hab/hudsonriver/Haverstraw_Bay.pdf|title=COASTAL FISH & WILDLIFE HABITAT RATING FORM: Haverstraw Bay|accessdate=2010-11-06|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20101126225828/http://nyswaterfronts.com/downloads/pdfs/sig_hab/hudsonriver/Haverstraw_Bay.pdf|archivedate=2010-11-26}}</ref> Up to the mid-1950s, Haverstraw Bay was once a productive [[oyster]] habitat.<ref>Stanne, S. et al., The Hudson:An Illustrated Guide to the Living River (Rutgers University Press/Clearwater, New Brunswick, 1996, p. 57)</ref> As with the rest of the Hudson, at the microbial level the bay's health is affected by oxygen concentrations. The bay's water chemistry is affected rain fall, tidal variations, and human induced waste and runoff, as well as by seasonal changes in temperature and light.<ref>[http://www.ldeo.columbia.edu/research/biology-paleo-environment/bpe-research/earth-microbiology/hudson-river-estuary Microbial Ecology of the Hudson River Estuary | Lamont–Doherty Earth Observatory<!-- Bot generated title -->]</ref>

== History ==
[[File:Sanford Robinson Gifford - Haverstraw Bay - 2011.43 - Cleveland Museum of Art.tiff|thumb|[[Sanford Robinson Gifford]]'s ''Morning in the Hudson, Haverstraw Bay'', 1866]]
In 1609, the [[Dutch East India Company]] had financed [[England|English]] navigator [[Henry Hudson]] to search for the [[Northwest Passage]]. In an attempt to find this undiscovered route, Henry Hudson decided to sail his ship up the [[river]] that would later be named after him ([[Hudson River]]). As he continued up the river, its width expanded, into Haverstraw Bay, leading him to believe he had successfully reached the Northwest Passage.

In 1780, spy [[John André|Major John André]] landed at Snedeker's Landing (a.k.a. Waldberg Landing) on the west shore of the bay in the woods below [[Haverstraw (village), New York|Haverstraw village]] to meet [[Benedict Arnold]].<ref>Adams, Arthur, The Hudson River Guidebook (Fordham University Press, New York, 1996, pp. 146)</ref>

In 1801, [[Charles Willson Peale]] traveled up the Hudson and sketched [[Stony Point, New York|Stony Point]] from the bay.

The bay appears in the 1975 [[James Lincoln Collier]] and [[Christopher Collier (historian)|Christopher Collier]] novel, ''[[My Brother Sam Is Dead]]''.

The bay is currently traversed by [[NY Waterway]]'s [[Haverstraw–Ossining Ferry]].
